summary:
The week of October 19-26, 2026 showed how routine, and how varied, local data center restrictions have become. On a single Tuesday (October 20), Volusia County, Florida gave final approval to a permanent ban on large-scale data centers in unincorporated areas — one of the first permanent county-level bans in the country — while Memphis's council rejected an 18-month moratorium on a 6-6 tie and instead passed a 135-day construction and application pause, Little Rock rejected a six-month moratorium on a 4-4 tie for the second time since August, Taunton, Massachusetts enacted a 365-day moratorium over a developer's objections, Cleveland extended its moratorium through January 2027, and Broward County, Florida voted to begin drafting a one-year moratorium. Later in the week, Clackamas County, Oregon (120 days, effective immediately) and Grant County, New Mexico (one year, notably covering dedicated power, water and transmission infrastructure, not just the data centers themselves) enacted county-wide moratoriums, and Calloway County, Kentucky approved a one-year pause. The split outcomes in Memphis and Little Rock underline that moratoriums are no longer automatic even where opposition is loud; councils facing multi-billion-dollar projects from Google and xAI are increasingly choosing short pauses, zoning overlays or outright rejection of restrictions over long freezes.
The regulatory toolkit is also maturing beyond simple pauses. Montgomery County, Tennessee (17-4) and Somerset County, Pennsylvania (unanimous) enacted detailed siting ordinances in the 500-to-1,000-foot-setback range with noise caps and utility-capacity proof requirements; Warrick County, Indiana is advancing a permanent Data Center Overlay district with a once-through cooling ban and peak-day water caps as Alcoa's ~700-acre Project Alloy approaches; and Sioux County, Iowa is set to replace its moratorium with a permanent zoning ordinance on October 27. Courts and administrative processes are becoming the next battleground: Archbald, Pennsylvania unanimously denied zoning for a 578-acre hyperscale campus after nine hearings (an appeal is expected), Urbana, Ohio rejected a settlement and will keep litigating a data center zoning suit with roughly $115 million in claimed damages at stake, and Wisconsin's DNR settled a Sierra Club suit by agreeing to a statewide strategic analysis of AI data center environmental impacts, due by January 2028 — a first-of-its-kind programmatic environmental review commitment at the state level.
At the state level, the most significant enacted development was in Pennsylvania, where Governor Shapiro signed SB 806, the AI Deceptive Advertising Act, on October 22 (Act 99 of 2026), requiring disclosure of AI-generated content in non-text advertising, while the House Communications & Technology Committee held a joint hearing October 19 on two competing frontier AI safety bills (HB 2800 and HB 2829) that would impose safety frameworks, audits and incident reporting on the largest model developers. New Jersey legislators introduced A 5663 and companion S 4659, which would prohibit new data center construction statewide until a DEP environmental impact study is complete, and an Assembly committee heard a three-bill AI disclosure and accountability package on October 19. In Virginia, Senator Russet Perry's prefiled SB 843 — a three-year statewide data center moratorium — heads toward the January 2027 session, and Loudoun County, the heart of the industry, deferred a 12-month application pause to November 17 after its county attorney advised a full moratorium would be illegal under state law.
Trends to watch: Governor Hochul's decision on New York's one-year permitting moratorium (effectively vetoed if unsigned by year-end); the November 3 ballot measures in Champaign County, Ohio (data center ban) and Boulder City, Nevada (whether to permit data centers in the Eldorado Valley); Broward County's and Loudoun County's November votes; and the January 2027 sessions in Virginia, Oregon and New Mexico, where statewide moratorium bills are queued. On the construction side, Epoch AI's latest assessment shows steady buildout continuing despite the political headwinds — Meta's Los Lunas, New Mexico campus brought a second building online (~147 MW) — even as the Financial Times reported at least 47 large US projects delayed, withdrawn or blocked in 2026.
